6 Safety-Related Structure, System, and Component Criteria and Capabilities
6.1 Design Requirements for Safety-Related Structures, Systems, and Components

Preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) section 6.1 describes the determination of structure,
system, and component (SSC)-specific design criteria and provides details of the analyses and
justifications for the development of safety-related design criteria (SRDC). PSAR section 6.1.1
discusses the design basis hazard levels (DBHLs), PSAR section 6.1.2 summarizes the SRDC,
and PSAR section 6.1.3 summarizes the DBHL-related requirements for non-safety-related
SSCs.

The applicable regulatory requirements for the design requirements for safety-related SSCs are
as follows:

e 10 CFR 50.34(a)(3)(ii)
10 CFR 50.34(a)(4)

The applicable guidance for the review of the design requirements for safety-related SSCs are
as follows:

e RG 1.76, Rev. 1, “Design-Basis Tornado and Tornado Missiles for Nuclear Power

Plants.” (ML070360253)

RG 1.115, Rev. 2, “Protection Against Turbine Missiles.” (ML101650675)

RG 1.189, Rev. 5, “Fire Protection for Nuclear Power Plants.” (ML23214A287)

 e DANU-ISG-2022-01, “Review of Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Advanced Reactor

6.1.1. Technical Evaluation

Design Basis Hazard Levels

The NRC staff reviewed the description of DBHLs in PSAR section 6.1.1 and table 6.1-1 using
applicable guidance in RG 1.233 and RG 1.253, which endorse, respectively, NEI 18-04 and,
with certain clarifications and additions, NEI 21-07. Per NEI 21-07, the construction permit (CP)
application content for section 6.1.1, should be as complete as possible based on the site
characterization required in 10 CFR 50.34(a). NEI 21-07 further states that DBHLs include both
external and internal hazards, such as seismic events, wind (including tornadoes and wind-
generated missiles), external flooding, hazards from external facilities, internal fires, internal
floods, high-energy line breaks, and internally generated missiles.

The NRC staff review determined that LME selected a set of DBHLs that is consistent with NEI
21-07. For each hazard, the NRC staff evaluated the information provided in the PSAR to
ensure it was reasonable to establish the design bases for protection against hazards for
applicable SSCs consistent with PDCs 2, 3, and 4. For the CP application, LME characterized
the external DBHLs using the results from PSAR Chapter 2, “Site Characteristics.” For internal
hazards that rely on final design information (e.g., internal fire, internal flood, HELB), the NRC
staff assessed the applicant’s plans to ensure safety significant SSCs will have appropriate
protection against these hazards at the operating license (OL) application stage. PSAR table
6.1-1 provides a summary of the DBHLs. The NRC staff's evaluation of each hazard is
described below.

Seismic Hazard

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 2.5.2, which addresses the seismic hazard at the LMGS
site, and PSAR sections 3.7, 3.8, 6.4, and 7.3, which describe the associated seismic analysis
methodology and design. The horizontal ground motion response spectrum (GMRS) for the
LMGS site has a peak ground acceleration (PGA) lower than 0.1g and therefore the safe
shutdown earthquake (SSE) horizontal design response spectrum was increased to achieve a
0.1g PGA in accordance with the minimum PGA required in Appendix S to Part 50. The NRC
staffs review of the LMGS seismic hazard and evaluation of the potential impact of a seismic
event on SSCs are provided in sections 2.5.2, 3.7, 3.8, 6.4, and 7.3 of this safety evaluation
(SE). In those sections, the NRC staff determined that LME has provided the necessary
information to address the design-basis seismic hazard and to support its evaluation of how the
design addresses the hazard.

Furthermore, as described in PSAR section 3.7.3.3, LME will perform a seismic probabilistic risk
assessment (SPRA) in support of a future OL application to confirm the overall seismic
performance and/or update seismic design criteria as necessary. Although not explicitly
considered in the DBHLs, sufficient seismic design margin would need to be demonstrated at
the OL application stage to meet the licensing modernization project (LMP) risk target for
beyond-design-basis events (BDBEs). The applicant’s preliminary approach is consistent with
the discussion in RG 1.253, Appendix A.3.7, which states that certain hazards (e.g., external
hazards such as seismic hazards) may be dispositioned at the CP stage by crediting DBHLs in

 lieu of explicitly modeling them in the PRA and evaluating their consequences. Consistent with
RG 1.253, the NRC staff will confirm the results are acceptable against the frequency-
consequence (F-C) target when the full scope PRA has been completed at the OL application
stage.

Based on the NRC staff's review of PSAR sections 2.5.2, 3.7, 3.8, 6.4, and 7.3 and its findings
documented in sections 2.5.2, 3.7, 3.8, 6.4, and 7.3 of this SE, respectively, the NRC staff
determined that the DBHL established for the seismic hazard is consistent with the design basis
seismic characteristics and is therefore consistent with PDC 2.

Wind Hazard (Tornado and Hurricane Loads and Generated Missiles)

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 2.3, table 2.0-1, and section 3.7, which provide the site-
specific parameters and applicant’s assessment of wind hazards. The wind hazard includes a
basic wind speed, a maximum wind speed bounded by the hurricane hazard, a pressure drop
and rate of pressure drop bounded by the tornado hazard, and tornado and hurricane generated
missiles generated from the missile spectra in RGs 1.76, Rev. 1 and RG 1.221. The NRC staff
determined, in sections 2.6 and 3.7 of this SE, that the site-specific wind hazard parameters and
associated applicant's assessment are consistent with RG 1.76, Rev. 1 and RG 1.221. Further,
the staff's review of PSAR section 6.1.1 and table 6.1-1 determined that the DBHL established
for wind hazard is consistent with the design basis wind parameters. On this basis and based on
the staff's determinations documented in sections 2.6 and 3.7 of this SE, the staff finds the wind
hazard DBHL meets the requirements of PDC 2.

External Flood

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 2.4.5.6, which provides flooding information for the
vicinity of the LMGS site. The DBHL flood level described in PSAR table 6.1-1 and PSAR table
2.0-1 is bounded by the probable maximum storm surge and includes a still water level and
wave run-up. PSAR section 6.1.1.4 describes LME’s approach to ensure adequate protection
against ingress of water into the buildings due to the flooding DBHL. The approach includes a
combination of strategies such as elevation protection (locating systems and components above
flood height), waterproof protection, and functional protection (submergence qualification).

The NRC staff determined that the DBHL established for external flooding is consistent with the
design basis external flood parameters (as documented in section 2.4 of this SE) and is
therefore consistent with PDC 2. Further, the NRC staff determined that the strategies to protect
safety-related (SR) SSCs against ingress of water due to external flooding are reasonable
because they account for the flooding DBHL flood height, the location of SSCs relative to the
flood height, and qualification of systems and components to withstand the effects of the
flooding DBHL, as needed, to ensure that they remain capable of performing their required
safety functions (RSFs).

Internal Fire

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.1.5, which states that, at the preliminary design
phase, fire related PDCs were identified to establish proper design requirements for SSCs. The
PSAR states that internal fire hazards will be fully evaluated at the OL application stage when
detailed SSC design and configurations are available. The fire scenario selection will include the

OFFICIAL USE ONLY — PROPRIETARY INFORMATHON

 identification of a fire ignition source (or set of fire ignition sources), secondary combustibles
and fire spread paths, fire damage targets, detection and suppression systems, and features to
be credited. PSAR section 8.6 provides additional discussion on fire protection and fire analysis.
PSAR sections 6.1.1.5 and 8.6 describe that the internal fire hazards and planned features will
be developed in conformance with applicable guidance, including RG 1.189, NFPA 804, and the
non-LWR PRA standard, which is endorsed by RG 1.247, with any deviations described and
justified.

The NRC staff determined that the internal fire hazard at LMGS is reasonably characterized for
the CP stage, and that planned features discussed in the PSAR are appropriate to ensure that
SR SSCs will maintain their safety-significant functions under postulated internal fire conditions,
consistent with PDC 3. The NRC staff will review LME’s evaluation of the fire protection features
at the OL application stage based on the final design information.

Internal Flood

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.1.6, which states that an internal flood event will be
expressed in terms of the specific flood source and its local impact. PSAR section 6.1.1.6
identifies potential design features to protect safety-significant SSCs from postulated flooding,
including isolation valves, physical barriers, and drains. The specific flood protection features
will be developed as part of the OL application. Additionally, at this preliminary stage, LME
identified several SR SSCs as not being subject to local flood sources. At the OL application
stage, LME will confirm that SSCs will either not be subject to any local flood source or will be
designed to not fail or challenge any RSFs.

The NRC staff determined that the internal flooding hazard at LMGS is reasonably
characterized for the CP stage, and that planned design measures discussed in the PSAR are
appropriate to ensure SR SSCs will maintain their safety-significant functions under postulated
internal flood conditions, in accordance with PDC 4. The NRC staff will review LME’s evaluation
of the necessary flood protection design features at the OL application stage based on the final
design information.

High-Energy Line Breaks (HELBs)

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.1.7, which states that HELB hazards are
characterized as a break of a pipe or piping system component containing a fluid maximum
operating temperature exceeding 200°F or a maximum operating pressure exceeding 275 psig.
Further, LME identified several SR SSCs that are either shielded from or are not subject to
HELB sources. PSAR section 6.1.1.7 states SR SSCs will be designed such that they will be
able to withstand or be protected from the impact of HELB missiles without any adverse impact
on their capability to perform required SR functions. The NRC staff will review analyses based
on the final design as part of a future OL application review to confirm that SR SSCs will be
capable of performing their functions. Design-basis pipe ruptures are addressed by one or more
of the following methods: physical separation, missile barriers, or demonstrating that HELB
missile impact does not adversely impact the ability of SR SSCs to perform their RSFs.

The NRC staff determined that the HELB hazard at LMGS is reasonably characterized for the
CP stage, and that planned design measures discussed in the PSAR are appropriate to ensure

OFFICIAL USE ONLY — PROPRIETARY INFORMATHON

 SR SSCs will maintain their safety-significant functions under postulated HELB conditions,
consistent with PDC 4. The staff will review LME’s evaluation of HELBs and their impacts at the
OL application stage based on the final design information and piping layout.

Turbine and Internally Generated Missiles

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.1.3, in which LME identified turbine missiles, other
missiles from rotating equipment, and secondary missiles outside the scope of the PRA for the
CP application. PSAR table 1.4-2 indicates that LME’s approach is consistent with RG 1.115
and will consider location and orientation of missile sources, missile generation frequency and
frequency of damage to SSCs, and the use of missile barriers. The final assessment of turbine
and internally generated missiles will be addressed at the OL application stage via an internal
hazards PRA. The NRC staff review determined that LME’s approach for the preliminary design
is appropriate to ensure SR SSCs will be adequately protected against turbine and other
internally generated missiles. The NRC staff will review LME’s evaluation of turbine and other
internally generated missiles and their impacts at the OL application stage based on the final
plant layout and design information.

Hazards From External Facilities

LME addressed hazards from external facilities in PSAR section 2.2. The NRC staff evaluated
these hazards in section 2.5 of this SE and concluded that LME has shown that hazards from
nearby external facilities and transportation routes are not expected to develop into a design-
basis hazard. The staff noted an exception related to general aviation aircraft crashes for which
LME committed to performing a final assessment of accidental aircraft hazards at the OL stage.
The NRC staff also noted that the preliminary assessment performed by LME is conservative
and determined that the review of the final assessment of accidental aircraft impact can be
reasonably left for the OL stage.

Based on its review of the preliminary assessments and design approaches discussed above,
the NRC staff finds that the DBHLs above are reasonable. This finding is based on LME’s
approach to defining the DBHLs for the preliminary design being consistent with the guidance in
RG 1.233, RG 1.253, and DANU-ISG-2022-01. As more detailed design and final information
becomes available, the applicant will further assess the internal flooding, internal fire, high-
energy line break hazards, hazards related to turbine and other internally generated missiles,
and hazards from external facilities, to confirm and update their associated DBHLs as
necessary and applicable. The staff will review LME’s final evaluation of the internal hazards at
the OL application stage, based on the final design information and plant layout.

Summary of SRDCs

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.2, which summarizes the SRDCs. The SRDCs are
used to map RSFs and required functional design criteria (RFDCs) to specific SR SSCs. LME
provided a list of SRDCs in PSAR table 6.1-2. Specifically, this table lists the SR SSCs, the
RSFs that the SR SSCs fulfill, and the RFDCs and SRDCs corresponding to each SR SSC. The
NRC staff review determined that the information provided in PSAR table 6.1-2 is consistent
with the guidance in section 6.1.2 of NEI 21-07 and therefore is acceptable. Further, the NRC
staffs review confirmed that the SRDCs listed in the table are addressed in the respective

 system subsections in PSAR chapter 6. The NRC staff's evaluation of the SRDCs is addressed
in the respective SR system discussions in section 6.4 of this SE.

Summary of DBHL-Related Requirements for Non-Safety-Related SSCs

The NRC staff evaluated PSAR section 6.1.3, which summarizes the DBHL-related
requirements for NSRST and NST SSCs. These requirements are applied to non-safety-related
SSCs to prevent adverse impacts on SR SSCs to perform their RSFs and do not affect the
safety classification of the SSCs (which are based on the functions that the SSCs perform within
the safety analysis). LME’s approach for preventing potential adverse impacts of non-safety-
related SSCs on the RSFs of SR SSCs includes physical separation, adjacent protection
barriers, or designing the SR SSCs to withstand physical or functional impact of the failure of
the NSRST or NST SSCs. Also, PSAR section 3.7 indicates that NSRST and NST SSCs are
classified as Seismic Category IIB and are designed to prevent adverse impacts on SR SSCs.
Additionally, the design criteria for NSRST structures include extreme tornado/hurricane design
loads and missile impacts in accordance with the concrete and steel nuclear codes and
standards and associated regulatory guides. The NRC staff review found LME’s approach for
preventing potential adverse impacts on SR SSCs to be consistent with the guidance in DANU-
ISG-2022-01.

A preliminary list of non-safety-related SSCs with DBHL-related requirements is provided in
PSAR table 6.1-3. Furthermore, PSAR section 6.1.3.8 describes LME’s process for identifying
additional NSRST and NST SSCs to which DBHL-related requirements must be applied to
prevent adverse impacts on the ability of SR SSCs to perform their RSFs. Per this process,
hazards sources are mapped to SR SSC targets by considering physical layouts, PSF functional
dependencies, prevention and mitigation capabilities, the availability of supporting equipment,
plant operating states, and plant work activities, among others. Primary sources and primary-
sources-dependent secondary sources are also considered. The process also includes
walkdown verifications. The NRC staff review finds this process to be systematic and thorough.
Further, the identification and evaluation of NSRST and NST SSCs that need DBHL
requirements is consistent with the guidance in RG 1.233 and RG 1.253.

Per PSAR section 3.7.3.1, a subset of NSRST SSCs are categorized as Seismic Category IIA
(SC-IIA) based their seismic risk significance consistent with the NEI 18-04 risk metrics. These
NSRST SSCs need to perform their function and meet the NEI 18-04 risk metrics during the
seismic DBHL. The staffs evaluation of the seismic design response spectra for these SSCs,
which are based on the seismic DBHL/SSE for the LMGS site, is addressed in section 3.7 of
this SE. Further, these NSRST SSCs are also protected from adverse interactions from other
NSRST or NST SSCs. The process for mapping hazard sources to these NSRST SSCs is
consistent with that used for SR SSCs. The NRC staff finds the hazards/sources mapping
process used for this NSRST SSCs to be acceptable because it is consistent with that used for
SR SSCs.

The NRC staff reviewed the PSAR section 6.1.3, which summarizes the DBHLs considered in
the determination of DBHL-related requirements for NSRST and NST SSCs. The NRC staff
review finds the scope of DBHLs described in PSAR section 6.1.3 to be consistent with those
identified in PSAR section 6.1.1. Moreover, PSAR section 6.1.3 describes that probabilistic
assessments will be performed as part of a future OL application to confirm or update the

OFFICIAL USE ONLY — PROPRIETARY INFORMATHON

 external DBHL-related requirements and develop the detailed internal DBHL-related
requirements. The NRC staff review finds LME’s approach to use probabilistic assessments in
the final selection of DBHLs to be consistent with RG 1.253, which endorses, with certain
Clarifications and additions, the alternative approaches for the selection of DBHLs described in
NEI 21-07, including deterministic and probabilistic approaches. The NRC staff will review the
final DBHL-related requirements for NSRST and NST SSCs at the OL application stage.

The NRC staff review also identified that certain NSRST and NST equipment and
instrumentation that may fail during the flooding DBHL require the development of strategies
and procedures to cope with their unavailability during the flooding DBHL for the LMGS site.
These NSRST and NST SSCs include equipment and instrumentation located in the controls
and electrical building (CEB). As described in PSAR section 6.1.3.4, LME mitigates the effects
of the potential unavailability of these supporting equipment and instrumentation via
implementation of its emergency plan and activation of the LMGS emergency response
organization. Per LME’s emergency plan, the plant is to be placed in a safe shutdown condition
either from the main control room (MCR) or from the reactor protection system (RPS) cabinets
located in the fuel handling auxiliary building (FHAB) if the MCR becomes unavailable due to
the external flood DBHL event. The staff notes that PSAR section 7.3.1.1.1 describes the design
requirements and strategies for protecting the FHAB and the SR SSCs within it from the
flooding DBHL. The staff's evaluation of such strategies is addressed in SE section 7.3.1. In the
case that the MCR becomes unavailable due to the external flood DBHL event, indications from
the RPS cabinets as well as portable monitoring equipment would be used to monitor the status
and radiological condition of the plant throughout the flooding event. Further, per PSAR section
6.1.3.4, LME will provide detailed emergency plans, emergency operating procedures, and
details associated with the portable monitoring equipment and indications at the OL application
stage. The NRC staff will review the emergency plan, operating procedures, and details
associated with the portable monitoring equipment and indications at the OL application stage.

PSAR chapter 8, “Plant Programs,” addresses, in part, the applicability of plant programs to
NSRST SSCs and the NRC staff's evaluation of these programs is in chapter 8 of this SE. The
application of DBHL requirements to NST SSCs that are necessary to ensure RSFs are
performed requires that certain programs be applied to NST SSCs to ensure the requirements
placed on those SSCs are met. Per PSAR section 6.1.3, the programmatic controls for NST
SSCs will be determined by the integrated decision-making process panel (IDPP) and may
include testing, maintenance, and/or inspection controls. Additionally, per PSAR section 8.1.3,
NST SSCs have QA requirements established based on ISO 9001. During the audit, the NRC
staff confirmed that LME’s process for establishing programmatic controls for NST SSCs
includes a condition evaluation to determine if additional programs or parts of programs should
be applied to NST SSCs. The NRC staff will evaluate the detailed programmatic requirements
applied to NST SSCs needing DBHL-related requirements at the OL stage.

6.1.2 Conclusion
Based on its review, the NRC staff finds that the information on DBHLs, SRDCs, and DBHL-
related requirements for NSRST and NST SSCs, described in PSAR Section 6.1, is consistent

with the applicable regulatory guidance listed above, and meets the relevant portions of 10
CFR 50.34(a)(3)(ii) and 10 CFR 50.34(a)(4). .

 6.2 Reliability and Capability Targets for Safety-Related Structures, Systems, and Components

PSAR section 6.2 describes the applicant’s approach to developing reliability and capability
targets for safety-related (SR) SSCs and presents the set of targets developed based on the
preliminary design.

The applicable regulatory requirements for the reliability and capability targets for SR SSCs are
as follows:

¢ 10 CFR 50.34(a)(4)
10 CFR 50.35(a)(1)

The applicable guidance for the review of PSAR section 6.2 is as follows:

e RG 1.233, “Guidance for a Technology Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and Performance-
Based Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for
Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” Rev. 0
(ML20091L698), which endorses, with clarifications, the guidance in NEI 18-04, “Risk-
Informed Performance-Based Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light Water
Reactor Licensing Basis Development,” Rev. 1 (ML19241A472).

e RG 1.253, Rev. 0, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive Content-of-Application
Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for Licenses,
Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” which endorses, with
clarifications and additions, NEI 21-07, “Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light
Water Reactor Safety Analysis Report: For Applicants Utilizing NEI 18-04 Methodology,”
Rev. 1 (ML22060A190).

6.2.3 Technical Evaluation

As described in PSAR section 1.3.1, the applicant is implementing the LMP methodology as
outlined in RG 1.233, which endorses, with clarifications, NEI 18-04. NEI 18-04 contains
guidance on defining the reliability and capability targets as part of the LMP methodology. As
described in PSAR chapter 1, LME is generally following the content and organization guidance
provided in NEI 21-07 and endorsed, with clarifications, in RG 1.253. NEI 21-07, Revision 1,
section C.6.2, “Reliability and Capability Targets for SR SSCs,” contains applicable guidance for
content and review of section 6.2 of the PSAR.

The NRC staff evaluated PSAR section 6.2 using the guidance in RG 1.233 and RG 1.253. As
described in NEI 18-04, reliability and capability targets are used to establish controls on the
frequency and consequence levels of non-DBA licensing basis events (LBEs) and to inform the
selection of special treatment requirements for SR and NSRST SSCs. LME provides preliminary
plant-level reliability and capability targets for SR SSCs in PSAR table 6.2-1 to meet the plant-
level safety objectives. The reliability and capability targets established ensure that the design

OFFICIAL USE ONLY — PROPRIETARY INFORMATHON

 supports the inputs and assumptions used by the safety analysis and to support staff findings
pursuant to 10 CFR 50.34(a)(4) and 50.35(a)(1).

The preliminary targets provided in the PSAR are limited to those for required safety functions
(RSFs) performed by SR SSCs that are explicitly modeled in the probabilistic risk assessment
(PRA) used to support the PSAR. As described in section 3.1.1 of this SE, the scope of this
PRA is limited to at-power internal events for the reactor, and some SSCs are not modeled
within the construction permit (CP) stage PRA. The NRC staff determined that limiting the
preliminary reliability and capability targets based on the PRA scope is sufficient for the CP
application given the preliminary design stage, the additional PRA development that would
occur between the CP and the operating license (OL), and LME’s commitment to follow the
guidance in the NEI 18-04 methodology, which includes defining reliability and capability targets
for all safety-significant SSCs.

PSAR Table 6.2-1, “Reliability and Capability Targets for SR SSCs,” of the PSAR defines the
preliminary reliability and capability targets for the following RSFs:

e RSF 1.1.1.2: Ensure sufficient inherent reactivity feedback by controlling primary heat
transport

RSF 1.1.2: Maintain long-term subcriticality

RSF 1.2.1: Maintain core heat removal through passive means

RSF 1.3.1: lsolate water/steam sources

RSF 1.4.1.1: Control primary pressure

The scope of RSFs identified in PSAR table 6.2-1 is a subset of the RSFs for the LMGS design
discussed in PSAR Section 5.2. The PSAR states that RSFs not included in the table are not
represented probabilistically in the PRA. The NRC staff notes that the RSFs not included in
PSAR table 6.2-1 are as follows:

e RSF 1.1.1.1: Ensure sufficient inherent reactivity feedback to maintain the core
radionuclide release limits to acceptable levels

e RSF 1.4.1.2: Limit stress in metallic core components

e RSF 1.4.2: Maintain reactor support geometry

NEI 18-04 states the purpose of the reliability and capability targets is to define the
requirements for the reliability and capability for SSCs modeled in the PRA. Therefore, the NRC
staff finds that the scope of the RSFs discussed in PSAR table 6.2-1, which is consistent with
the scope of RSFs modeled in the PRA at the CP stage, is consistent with RG 1.233, which
endorses, with clarifications, NEI 18-04. As noted above, while some SSCs are not modeled
within the current PRA, the PRA will continue to develop from CP to OL and SSCs that play a
role in preventing or mitigating LBEs would be incorporated into the PRA prior to the OL
application.

 The applicant proposed the following reliability targets for each RSF listed in PSAR table 6.2-1:

e Maintain frequency of all LBEs with failure of the RSF below 1E-4 per plant calendar
year.

e Maintain LBEs with failure of the RSF within the F-C target.

e Maintain cumulative risk metrics within targets.

The applicant stated that the basis for the functional-level reliability targets is derived from the
development of frequency targets for a collection of LBEs that are prevented or mitigated by a
particular RSF. However, the reliability targets listed above from PSAR table 6.2-1 align with the
overall requirements that the plant must meet, without further definition of the reliability various
functions will need to achieve. Therefore, because the reliability targets align with the overall
plant requirements, the NRC staff determined that the preliminary reliability targets defined are
aligned with plant level targets, as defined in section 6.2 of NEI 21-07.

NEI 21-07 states that reliability and capability targets can be established at different levels: plant
level, functional level, or SSC level. Thus, the applicant’s approach of establishing plant-level
targets at the CP stage with a defined methodology for establishing functional and SSC-level
targets at the OL stage is consistent with RG 1.253, which endorses, with certain clarifications
and additions, NEI 21-07. The plant-level targets are discussed further in PSAR chapter 3,
“Methodologies, Analyses, and Licensing Basis Events,” and chapter 4, “Integrated
Evaluations,” associated with the frequency-consequence target and cumulative risk metrics.

The LME process for developing functional- and system-level reliability targets from the plant-
level targets is described in PSAR section 6.2. This process involves associating the functions
with the LBEs they impact and then optimizing the set as a whole to determine the frequency
target for each function that maximizes margin between the PRA modeled performance and the
target performance impacting the conclusions of the safety analysis. The results from exercising
this method for setting reliability targets will be evaluated at the OL application stage consistent
with NEI 21-07. The applicant also states that the Final Safety Analysis Report (FSAR)
submitted as part of a future OL application will describe system-level reliability and capability
targets.

The applicant also proposed a capability target for each RSF identified in PSAR table 6.2-1. The
PSAR states that the capability target is informed by the success criteria used in the PRA to
determine success or failure of a particular RSF at the functional level and aligns with the
corresponding reliability target.

The NRC staff reviewed the proposed preliminary reliability and capability targets and
determined them to be reasonable and acceptable based on the following:

6.4.2.1 Technical Evaluation

Safety Significance

The fuel design plays a significant role in safety for the Xe-100 reactor due to its importance as
the primary functional containment barrier for radionuclide retention, its role in heat removal,
and the Xe-100 reliance on inherent reactivity feedback as a primary shutdown mechanism.

The performance of the fuel as the radionuclide retention barrier reduces reliance on other
functional containment mechanisms such as confinement or containment barriers around the
reactor which traditionally require active detection and isolation or filtration, which has varying
levels of effectiveness depending on the radionuclides present. Alternatively, the functional
containment barrier provided by TRISO fuel provides robust passive layers of protection that
have historically been shown to remain effective over a wide range of temperature. The primary
challenge to this radionuclide retention barrier comes in the form of temperature, shifting safety
review focus from traditional detection and isolation to control of temperature through heat
generation and heat removal.

The reliance on inherent reactivity feedback as a primary shutdown mechanism was evaluated
based on a variety of factors. The first factor was that inherent reactivity feedback is not a
function of the fuel alone. The reactivity of a system and its response to changes (i.e., reactivity
feedback) is a function of the type of fuel, the arrangement of fuel, the material and arrangement
of reflectors and moderators, the temperatures within the system, structural materials that
impact absorption, etc. Reactivity is a system-wide characteristic and understanding the roles
the fuel plays in that system and the impact that changes in the fuel can have on that system
are key to understanding the safety significance of the fuel design relative to the inherent
reactivity feedback of the system.

A second factor evaluated with respect to the inherent reactivity feedback was that inherent
reactivity feedback cannot shut down the system or maintain the system in a low power or
shutdown state unless the temperature of the system remains high (i.e., heat removal is
restricted). This puts the fundamental safety function of controlling heat generation (i.e.,
reactivity and power) at odds with the fundamental safety function of controlling heat removal,
which is generally thought of as maximizing heat removal. These key factors were evaluated
along with other safety considerations important to the design of the fuel as part of this review.
